chapters.title: Chapter 3: Central Bank Coordination and Divergence

lessons.title: When Central Banks Move Together: The 2022 Synchronized Tightening Cycle

body.text: Most of the time, the world's major central banks move on different clocks: one hiking while another eases. 2022 broke that pattern. Nearly every major central bank hiked at once, and that synchronization amplified the global liquidity contraction far beyond what any single central bank could have caused alone.

children.text: When only one major central bank tightens while others stay easy, capital has somewhere to go. Money leaving dollar assets can still find a home in easy-money euros or yen. In 2022, that escape valve mostly disappeared. Inflation had become a genuinely global problem, driven by post-COVID demand, supply chain disruption, and the energy shock from Russia's invasion of Ukraine, and central bank after central bank responded with the same medicine at the same time.

events.title: The Fed's First Hike of the Cycle
events.description: The Fed raises rates for the first time since 2018, ending pandemic-era near-zero rates and signaling the start of its fastest hiking cycle in decades.

events.title: The RBI Hikes Too
events.description: The RBI raises its repo rate in an off-cycle move, its first hike in nearly four years, starting a domestic tightening cycle that runs alongside the Fed's, not behind it.

events.title: The Fed's 75 Basis Point Hikes
events.description: The Fed delivers multiple consecutive 75 basis point hikes, a pace not seen in decades, while the Bank of England and other major central banks hike in parallel.

events.title: The ECB Hikes for the First Time Since 2011
events.description: The European Central Bank raises rates for the first time in over a decade, ending its own era of negative and near-zero rates and joining the synchronized move.

events.title: Nearly the Whole World Had Tightened
events.description: The Fed, ECB, Bank of England, RBI and most other major central banks had all raised rates substantially within the same calendar year, an unusually synchronized tightening cycle by historical standards.

stats.label: Fed, Cumulative 2022 Hikes
stats.context: From near zero to roughly 4.25-4.50% by year end, the fastest pace since the early 1980s.

stats.label: ECB, Cumulative 2022 Hikes
stats.context: From 0% to roughly 2.5% by year end, its first hikes since 2011.

stats.label: RBI, Cumulative FY23 Hikes
stats.context: Repo rate raised from 4% to roughly 6.25% over the tightening cycle that began in May 2022.

body.text: Rate hike figures above are approximate cumulative totals for illustration. Exact meeting-by-meeting decisions are available from the Fed, ECB and RBI directly.

children.text: Why Synchronization Hurts Emerging Markets More

body.text: When every major reserve currency is tightening at once, there is no offsetting easy-money pocket for global capital to rotate into. The dollar strengthens broadly against nearly everything at the same time, not just against currencies whose own central bank is lagging. For a commodity-importing economy like India, that broad-based dollar strength lands as a double hit: imported inflation rises through costlier oil and other dollar-priced commodities, at the very moment capital outflow pressure is also building. Both channels push the same direction together, which is what makes a synchronized tightening cycle materially more painful than an ordinary divergence.

body.label: US Dollar Index (DXY), 2022 Peak
body.context: A roughly two-decade high, reflecting broad-based dollar strength against nearly every major currency at once, not just against laggards.

children.text: Synchronization vs Divergence: Why the Distinction Matters

body.caption: How Central Bank Synchronization Changes the Picture for India

cells: Broad-based, against nearly all major currencies
Money can rotate into still-easy currencies
Few easy-money currencies left to rotate into
Moderate, tied mainly to dollar strength alone
Amplified, tied to both dollar strength and global commodity prices
More room to lag or diverge from the Fed

body.title: Stronger Fundamentals, Still a Painful Year
body.scenario: Going into 2022, India's current account deficit and forex reserve position were both far stronger than they had been in 2013. Yet 2022 was still a difficult year for the rupee and for FPI flows, even if less disruptive than the 2013 taper tantrum.
body.prompt: Given India's much-improved starting position, why wasn't 2022 a non-event, and what does the synchronization angle add to the explanation beyond what you learned about India's 2013 vulnerabilities?
body.modelAnswer: Stronger fundamentals reduced the severity of the shock but did not eliminate it, because the 2022 shock was structurally different from 2013. In 2013, the problem was largely India-specific vulnerability, a large current account deficit financed by hot money, meeting a Fed-only policy shift. In 2022, nearly every major central bank tightened together, producing broad-based dollar strength and simultaneous global commodity inflation that no amount of domestic balance sheet improvement alone could fully offset, since the shock was hitting through two channels at once (imported inflation and capital outflow pressure) rather than one. India's stronger starting position meant it absorbed this broader shock better than it would have in 2013 condition, but a synchronized global shock is a different animal from a single-country vulnerability, and better fundamentals cushion it rather than cancel it.

body.title: Check Your Understanding
body.question: Why does a synchronized tightening cycle, where nearly all major central banks hike together, tend to hurt emerging markets more than a divergent one?
options: Because synchronized hikes are always larger in absolute size than divergent ones
Because there is no easy-money currency left for capital to rotate into, and dollar strength becomes broad-based rather than selective
Because emerging market central banks are legally required to follow the Fed exactly
Because synchronized tightening always causes a recession in the US
body.explanation: When every major reserve currency tightens together, capital has nowhere easy to rotate into, and the dollar strengthens broadly against nearly everything at once. For commodity-importing emerging markets like India, that combines with global commodity inflation to create a double hit that a single-bank divergence does not produce.

points: 2022 was unusual because nearly every major central bank (Fed, ECB, Bank of England, RBI and others) tightened within the same calendar year, a rare synchronization rather than the more typical divergence.
Synchronized tightening removes the easy-money currency that capital would normally rotate into, making dollar strength broad-based rather than selective.
For a commodity-importing economy like India, synchronized global tightening lands as a double hit: imported inflation and capital outflow pressure moving in the same direction at once.
Stronger fundamentals, as India had in 2022 versus 2013, cushion a synchronized shock but do not cancel it, because the shock itself is structurally broader.
The distinction between synchronization and divergence, covered in the rest of this chapter, is central to reading how much room the RBI actually has to set its own independent policy path.
